Guide: Analysing dynamic stability

Source: vignettes/guide-analyse-stability.qmd

This guide gives an overview of the experimental tools for analysing the dynamic stability of a mizer steady state and characterising the limit cycles that can replace it. For full documentation of each function, follow the links.

Tools for asking whether a mizer steady state is dynamically stable — and, when it is not, characterising the limit cycle that replaces it. These are experimental: their interface may still change. findSteadyState(solver = "newton") assumes the standard semichemostat resource dynamics and solves for the resource alongside the fish, so the resource density and the feeding levels it implies are self-consistent even where consumers are satiated. getStability() and getDiscreteStability() include every supported dynamic resource coordinate alongside the fish. Continuous analysis needs a resource equation capability; discrete analysis uses the supported resource step. Both require an appropriate autonomous-model contract for the providers used by the analysis.

Distinct from calibration: the guide to reaching steady state and calibrating gets you onto a fixed point; what follows analyses the dynamics around it. The natural entry point is findSteadyState(params, solver = "newton"), which converges even when the fixed point is dynamically unstable, unlike the default solver = "project".

Is the steady state stable? — getStability()

getStability(params) computes the continuous-time eigenvalues of the model. Mizer discretises the size axis but not time, so on the size grid the model is a system of ODEs; getStability() differentiates their right-hand side directly and takes the eigenvalues of that Jacobian. No time step is involved, so the eigenvalues are a property of the model rather than of a solver. The result reports whether the state is stable, unstable or inconclusive, the maximum real part of the eigenvalues (max_real_part; > 0 means unstable), and the period at which the model rings (dominant_period for the dominant mode, oscillation_period for the leading oscillatory one). A complex pair is an oscillatory mode, not a bifurcation: its period is the period of an emerging limit cycle only where its real part is zero, which is a Hopf bifurcation and which a single spectrum cannot show. Watch Re(leading_oscillatory_eigenvalue) cross zero over a scanModel() before calling one. It also returns leading_eigenvectors, the top two eigenvectors of the state space split into $fish, a complex array (n_species, n_sizes, 2), and $resource, a complex matrix (n_w_full, 2), each normalised to maximum modulus 1 (the spatial shape of the oscillation).

params <- findSteadyState(params, solver = "newton")  # sit exactly on the (possibly unstable) fixed point
stab   <- getStability(params)
stab                                     # stable/unstable, growth rate, cycle period
  • effort sets the fishing effort used when forming the Jacobian.
  • h is the relative finite-difference step. Re-running with a different h is the cheapest check that the model is smooth enough for the analysis to mean anything: if the answer moves, do not trust it.

Both getStability() and getOscillationModeSim() use the state stored in the object. At a state that fails its scoped steady-state assessment, raw Jacobian diagnostics do not establish equilibrium stability: the verdict is inconclusive. getOscillationModeSim() requires complete, current support and an autonomous equilibrium for its recorded scope. Run findSteadyState() or tuneSteadyState() first, then inspect getSteadyAssessment() — see the guide to reaching steady state and calibrating. An old stability list without coverage and scope must be recomputed.

tuneSteadyState() and findSteadyState() attach a related "convergence" attribute, which answers three questions separately: termination says why the run stopped, converged whether the solver met its own criterion, and attractor what the state reached actually is — "fixed_point", "limit_cycle" or NA. Read attractor together with assessment: a fixed-point label requires the measures for its recorded scope to pass. residual remains a separate biomass-drift diagnostic. An explicitly conditional fixed point is not a whole-model equilibrium claim.

Stopping on a fixed point takes both a distance function below distance_tol and every required assessment passing; missing assessment support stops the operation before the search. Limit cycles are detected from the per-species biomass series sampled at every time step, at every check rather than only when the distance criterion has failed, because a cycle whose period divides t_check is sampled at one phase and looks converged. The relative-amplitude floor for calling an oscillation a cycle is the amplitude_tol argument (default 0.01).

What the analysis covers

getSteadyAssessment() and isSteady() cover the whole model by default, including registered component assessments. A conditional request names the states held fixed, and its scope stays attached to the result. The current Newton solver can solve consumers and resource only; dynamic component states must be explicitly held fixed when using it. The projection solver can advance components, provided their convergence measures are declared.

Stability means the whole model by default. Dynamic component Jacobians are not available in this release, so a model containing an uncovered dynamic component returns an incomplete, inconclusive report. It does not silently compute a subsystem and label it as the whole model. Request the subsystem explicitly when that is the question you want to ask:

stab <- getStability(params, scope = "conditional", fixed = "component:pool")
stab$scope
stab$coverage

The fixed owners remain recorded throughout the result and any generated oscillation-mode simulation. A fixed dynamic pool is different from an input declared by the model. Explicit prescribed-input declarations, including coordinate masks for partially prescribed states, remove those coordinates from both continuous and discrete eigenproblems. Built-in resource_constant declares the resource as prescribed. Excluded coordinates are reconstructed as zero perturbations in eigenvectors and stay unchanged in mode simulations.

Mizer never decides that a coordinate is prescribed because its abundance, derivative or Jacobian row happens to be zero. Entirely absent fish species still have invasion modes, and genuine zero eigenvalues or unit multipliers remain in the spectrum. This differs from the active set used by the Newton solver.

Read status, stable, coverage and assessment together:

Evidence for the requested scope status stable
Complete autonomous equilibrium, all modes strictly decay stable TRUE
Complete autonomous equilibrium, a mode grows unstable FALSE
Marginal modes, missing support, or a non-equilibrium state inconclusive NA
Complete coverage with no dynamic coordinates not_applicable NA

stability_tol sets the numerical margin around zero real part or unit modulus. The result records this tolerance, the evaluation time, prescribed coordinates, conditional exclusions and reasons for missing support. Time-dependent forcing needs its own suitable analysis; a stationary state alone does not establish that its Jacobian is autonomous. isTRUE(stab$stable) safely tests for an established stable verdict.

Is mizer’s time step stable? — getDiscreteStability()

A different question, and the one to ask when a simulation disagrees with getStability(). getDiscreteStability(params, dt = 1) linearises the one-step map that project(method = "euler") takes at that step size and returns its discrete_eigenvalues and spectral_radius. Below 1 means the numerical scheme does not amplify perturbations at that dt. It is that step and not an approximation to it: the same transport coefficients, the same Thomas solver and the model’s own resource_dynamics.

With excluded coordinates, this is the full step with those inputs reset to their reference values between steps, followed by selection of the dynamic outputs. It is not a newly derived numerical solver for the constrained continuous equations; an implicit step can couple coordinates internally.

The two verdicts can differ, and that is the point: the implicit transport solve damps oscillations artificially, so an unstable steady state can have a spectral radius below 1 at a large dt and a simulation will then settle onto a state the model does not hold. If getStability() says unstable but the simulation goes flat, check getDiscreteStability() at the dt you are projecting with, and reduce dt (or use method = "second_order").

The discrete eigenvalues cannot be converted into continuous ones by any exact algebraic relation, because mizer’s step is not fully implicit: the rates are evaluated at the state at the start of the step and only the transport solve is implicit. That is why getStability() differentiates the rates of change directly instead of inverting the one-step map.

Visualising the oscillation — getOscillationModeSim()

getOscillationModeSim(params) takes the output of findSteadyState() and builds a MizerSim covering exactly one period of the leading oscillatory mode in the linear approximation,

[ x(t) = x^* + A,!, ]

over the whole state (x = (N, n_{pp})), where (v) is getStability()’s leading_oscillatory_eigenvector — the eigenvector of the dominant oscillatory mode, which is not in general the dominant mode — and (A) is scaled so that the largest relative swing in species biomass equals the amplitude argument (default 10%): the hardest-oscillating species departs that far from its steady biomass and no species departs further. Fish and resource share one (A), so the resource oscillates with the phase the mode gives it; on NS_params at effort 1.5 it leads the fish biomass by about 0.3 years of the 5.12-year period. The growth factor (e^{t}) is deliberately omitted so the oscillation closes after one period; the run ends exactly at (T), with a shortened final interval when t_save does not divide it, so the last state is the first state again. () is recorded as growth_rate in the result’s sim_params, and it is what decides whether this is a cycle the model settles onto or a transient it rings with on the way back.

A biomass amplitude does not bound the individual size classes — a cohort trough is a far larger relative excursion than the biomass integral over it — so getOscillationModeSim() reports when the perturbation drives an abundance negative and it has to be clipped at zero. On NS_params at effort 1.5 that starts at around amplitude = 0.2. Past that point the picture is no longer the linear mode. The result is an ordinary MizerSim, so plot it with the standard tools (see the guide to analysing and plotting mizer results):

params <- findSteadyState(params, solver = "newton")
sim    <- getOscillationModeSim(params, amplitude = 0.1)
plotBiomass(sim)                         # biomass oscillation over one period
animate(plotSpectra(sim))               # the travelling wave in the spectrum

This is the linear mode — the shape near onset. For the fully nonlinear cycle, project the real dynamics with the second-order scheme (see the guide to running a mizer simulation).

Where does the cycle appear? — scanModel()

scanModel() sweeps any aspect of the model and, at each value, follows the attractor of the full dynamics and records the long-term range of a summary quantity. Draw that range with style = "envelope" and you have a bifurcation diagram: a stable steady state shows as a single line, a limit cycle as a band between its minimum and maximum, so a Hopf bifurcation appears as the value at which the band opens up.

scan <- scanModel(params, scan_values = seq(0, 1.5, 0.05),
                  set_func = scanEffort(), value_func = getYield)
plot(scan, style = "envelope")
  • set_func says what to vary — scanEffort() for the fishing effort of every gear together, scanFishingMortality() for the fishing mortality on one species, scanSpeciesParam() for any species parameter. value_func says what to measure: any of getBiomass(), getYield(), getSSB(), getN(). species restricts which series are shown. See the guide to analysing and plotting mizer results.
  • The settling stage runs projectUntilSettled(), whose distance_tol, residual_tol, amplitude_tol and extinction_threshold are exposed for tuning when a run is slow to settle or a species is collapsing.
  • The returned MizerScan object is a data frame, so the numbers behind the diagram are available without re-running the scan.

Reading and subsetting a scan

The first two columns of a MizerScan have dynamic names: column 1 is named by scan_name (for example, "Fishing effort"), and column 2 by value_name (for example, "Yield"). Read them by position in reusable code, or obtain their names with names(scan)[1:2]:

scanned <- scan[[1]]
measured <- scan[[2]]
fixed <- scan[scan$attractor %in% "fixed_point", ]
plot(fixed)

The other columns have fixed names: Species identifies the series; ymin and ymax give its range; attractor is "fixed_point", "limit_cycle" or NA; termination and converged describe how the run stopped; and period and residual report the cycle period and remaining biomass drift. Use attractor, rather than converged alone, to identify equilibrium or cycle results.

Use [ for row subsetting. It preserves the plotting metadata and recomputes at_max and max_value from the remaining rows. Keep the first three columns in their original order if you also select columns and want the result to remain a MizerScan. Base subset() also preserves this metadata for row selection. Other data-frame operations can drop it or leave derived attributes stale: transform() drops the scan wrapper, while dplyr::filter() can retain it without refreshing the recorded maxima. For arbitrary data manipulation, use as.data.frame(scan) and make your own plot, or rebuild with MizerScan() and the original metadata before using plot() on the scan again.

Comparing forward and backward sweeps

With continuation = TRUE (the default), each value starts from the state reached at the preceding value. This can reveal hysteresis when a model has coexisting attractors: an increasing and a decreasing sweep can follow different stable branches at the same parameter values.

Start from models settled near the two ends of the range, with initial states in the basins of the branches you want to follow. Set the endpoint’s scanned parameter and settle it with findSteadyState(), which keeps model parameters fixed. tuneSteadyState() recalibrates reproduction and the resource, so independently tuned endpoints may no longer describe the same model. Here params_low and params_high have the same model parameters apart from fishing effort:

values <- seq(0, 1.5, 0.05)
up <- scanModel(params_low, scan_values = values,
                set_func = scanEffort(), value_func = getSSB,
                continuation = TRUE, current_scan_value = NULL)
down <- scanModel(params_high, scan_values = rev(values),
                  set_func = scanEffort(), value_func = getSSB,
                  continuation = TRUE, current_scan_value = NULL)
plot(up, style = "envelope")
plot(down, style = "envelope")

Leaving current_scan_value = NULL preserves the supplied scan order. Giving it a value, including "auto", instead sweeps outwards from that value, restarting from the supplied model in each direction. continuation = FALSE restarts every point from the supplied initial model, so it does not follow the preceding branch.

An abrupt jump between branches can indicate a saddle-node fold. Check attractor, termination and residual near the jump, allow enough time to settle, and refine scan_values there before interpreting it as a threshold. These are sweeps of the dynamics: they follow attracting states, not the unstable branch between them, and do not locate a fold exactly. The params attribute of a scan holds its starting model, not the final state of the sweep; it cannot be used as the settled starting state for a reverse sweep.

Numerical caveat

getStability() involves no time step, so the temporal numerical diffusion of the implicit solver does not enter its answer at all. But the spatial numerical diffusion from the default first-order upwind scheme does: it is part of the semi-discretised model that the eigenvalues describe. A real limit cycle can still be damped to a flat line by the spatial scheme alone!

To accurately simulate the fully nonlinear oscillation and confirm a stable cycle, build the model with second_order_w = TRUE and project with method = "second_order". See the guide to running a mizer simulation.
